challenged_premise.text: The truth about, and knowledge of, a free choice depends upon that actual choice (Grounding Principle).

objection: Imagine a man named Elias who chooses to drink water at noon. According to the Grounding Principle, the truth of this choice and the knowledge of it are grounded in Elias's act. If God's knowledge of Elias's choice depends on that contingent act, then God's knowledge is not identical to His necessary essence. Since God is absolutely simple, His knowledge is His being. If His knowledge is grounded in a creature's choice, then God's very existence becomes contingent upon the world, violating divine simplicity and aseity.

strongest_responses.response: Defender A distinguished between grounding the truth of God's knowledge in a creature's act and grounding God's essence or existence in that act, arguing that on the eternalist picture the dependence runs from the temporal object to the relation of knowing rather than from creation into the divine nature.
strongest_responses.why_it_failed: The objector pressed that if God's knowledge is identical to His essence, any dependence of that knowledge on a contingent act is necessarily a dependence of the essence itself, and Defender A conceded that the original argument lacks the explicit extrinsicness clause needed to block this inference.

strongest_responses.response: Defender A appealed to Aquinas-style accounts on which God's knowing of creatures is a relation of reason that leaves God really unchanged, proposing that the truth-value of the knowledge is a fact about the object and the relation rather than a further determination of the essence.
strongest_responses.why_it_failed: It got some distance in mapping how the dependence might be merely extrinsic, yet it ultimately failed to vindicate the original argument because it required introducing a new premise that the text did not state.

open_questions: Can a truth-conditional dependence of divine knowledge on creaturely acts be consistently classified as merely extrinsic if that knowledge is identical to the divine essence?
Does the eternalist thesis that all time is present to God suffice to block the inference from the contingency of the object known to any contingency in the divine essence?
Is a revised Grounding Principle that includes an explicit extrinsicness clause still compatible with the original motivation for linking divine foreknowledge to libertarian free will?
paper_direction: A paper here would argue that the Grounding Principle can be reformulated with an explicit extrinsicness clause so that the truth of divine knowledge depends on creaturely free choices without compromising divine simplicity or aseity. The case would develop a metaphysics of eternalist divine cognition on which the truth-conditions of God's knowledge are fixed by temporal objects through a real relation of reason that leaves the divine essence intrinsically unchanged, drawing on the distinction between the content of knowledge and the ontological ground of the knower. The strongest reply to anticipate is that if God's knowledge is identical to His essence, any truth-conditional dependence on contingent acts necessarily renders the essence itself contingent, a challenge the paper must meet by showing that extrinsic relationality to contingent objects does not introduce contingency into the essence of a simple being. To succeed, the paper would need to show not merely that this distinction is coherent, but that it is already implicit in the eternalist framework and can be stated without collapsing into the very modal dependence the objector identifies.

reasons.coherence: The objection does not show the Grounding Principle false; it shows a tension with divine simplicity, which is not a premise of the argument. The direction also conflates Aquinas's distinction (a relation of reason on God's side, real on the creature's side) into a 'real relation of reason,' so it is aimed at an imported commitment and stated loosely.
reasons.robustness: The obvious replies are prior art (Grant's extrinsic model) and the point that the simplicity problem is independent of eternalism and grounding. The direction neither anticipates nor answers these, and its requirement that the clause be 'already implicit in eternalism' is unsupported.
reasons.significance: Even if it succeeded, it would at best attach a known Thomist move to Rogers's reply to Hasker. It would leave the actual reconciliation dispute about eternity, accidental necessity and Hasker's objections untouched.
reasons.specificity: There is a definite thesis (a GP with an extrinsicness clause) and an identified objection to meet, but no concrete account of what makes a dependence 'extrinsic,' and no plan for the cross-world intrinsic-sameness problem.

assessment.strongest_objection: The proposal is not novel, and its distinctive element does no work. The extrinsic model of divine knowing is already worked out and contested in W. Matthews Grant's 'Divine Simplicity, Contingent Truths, and Extrinsic Models of Divine Knowing' (2012), in Brower's work on simplicity and truthmaking, and in the Mullins/Tomaszewski modal-collapse literature. The contingent-knowledge problem for simplicity also arises for any contingent divine knowledge, such as knowledge of what God creates, whether or not God is eternal or the Grounding Principle holds. So neither eternalism nor a reformulated GP is doing work, and the paper would reduce to restating the Thomist/Grant view inside Rogers's framework.
assessment.what_it_needs: The paper must engage the existing extrinsic-model literature directly. It must show something specific to the eternalist, libertarian Grounding Principle, for example that grounding by free creaturely acts creates a dependence problem that grounding by God's own contingent creative will does not, and that the proposed clause handles it. Otherwise it should be recast as a contribution to the simplicity debate, not to the foreknowledge reconciliation.
assessment.summary: This is a rediscovery of the existing extrinsic-model debate about simplicity and contingent knowledge, aimed at a premise whose truth it does not actually challenge; without engaging Grant and showing something specific to eternalist grounding, a competent reader would dismiss it.

revision.research_question: On an eternalist, libertarian reading of the Grounding Principle, can the truth-conditions of divine foreknowledge depend on creaturely free choices without making the divine essence contingent? Does eternalism, rather than the simplicity problem as such, change how that dependence must be stated?
revision.paper_direction: A paper here would argue that, for the eternalist and libertarian Grounding Principle, the dependence of divine knowledge on a free creaturely act is a dependence of truth-value on the act, not of the divine essence on the act. The paper engages the existing extrinsic-model literature directly, including Grant's treatment of contingent truths under divine simplicity, rather than treating it as background. Its specific contribution concerns the eternalist, libertarian case. Grounding by God's own contingent creative will is an intra-divine dependence on a will that God freely exercises, so the essence is not made to depend on anything outside itself. Grounding by free creaturely acts is different. Those acts must be open under the Anselmian thesis, so the grounding relation cannot be read as causal or sequential. On an eternal view, God's knowing is not located before the act, so no temporal or causal dependence of the knower is available. The paper argues that the grounding relation must therefore be restricted to the propositional content of divine knowledge, and it states this with an extrinsicness clause. The clause specifies that the relation holds between a proposition about God's knowing and the creaturely act, and that it does not hold between the act and the divine knowing relation or essence. Conditional necessities of the form 'if X then X' are used to show that this truth-conditional dependence does not make the knowing relation contingent. The paper treats the generic simplicity worry, which also arises for knowledge of what God creates, as a distinct and prior problem. It addresses that worry through the extrinsic model and does not claim the eternalist framing solves it. The paper's claim is limited: eternalism and the libertarian reading of the Grounding Principle require a specific extrinsicness clause, and that clause is what allows foreknowledge to be reconciled with open choices, which bears on the reconciliation dispute with Hasker's objections.
revision.reply_to_strongest_objection: The paper concedes that the simplicity problem for contingent knowledge is generic and was already treated in the extrinsic-model literature, so it does not claim novelty for the simplicity point. Its distinct claim is narrower. The paper separates two grounding sources. Grounding by God's contingent creative will is intra-divine. Grounding by free creaturely acts is not, and under the Anselmian thesis those acts are open, so the dependence must be stated as a dependence of truth-value on the act. The extrinsicness clause makes that statement: the relation holds between the act and the propositional truth of divine knowledge, not between the act and the knowing relation or essence. The paper then uses the internal-necessity principle ('if X then X') to show that the resulting conditional structure introduces no contingency into the essence. This is an argument specific to the eternalist, libertarian Grounding Principle, and it engages the reconciliation dispute rather than restating the Thomist view.
revision.what_changed: The revision narrows the thesis from a general reformulation of the Grounding Principle to a claim about the eternalist, libertarian case, where the grounding must be stated as truth-dependence through an explicit extrinsicness clause, and it engages the existing extrinsic-model literature directly.

reasons.coherence: The simplicity objection is consistent and does press on the Grounding Principle as stated, but it attacks a premise (absolute simplicity) that the reconstructed argument never asserts; the proposal then partly answers it with an asymmetry (God's will versus creaturely acts) that is incoherent under the very simplicity it grants.
reasons.robustness: The obvious reply is that the eternalist, libertarian case reduces to the generic extrinsic model; the direction concedes the generic point but offers no argument that eternalism changes what the clause must say, and its extra tools (the will contrast, the 'if X then X' necessity) do not do the work assigned to them.
reasons.significance: Even if it succeeded, the paper would mostly relocate an existing extrinsic-model solution into the Rogers–Hasker exchange, which is a modest clarification of how Rogers must state the Grounding Principle rather than a new move in the foreknowledge debate.
reasons.specificity: There is a definite thesis (restrict grounding to the truth-value of propositions about divine knowing via an explicit clause) and an outline of steps, but the key distinction between a proposition about God's knowing and the knowing relation is never fixed precisely enough to be tested, and the literature base is thin and largely irrelevant (Molina, a Leibniz review).

assessment.strongest_objection: The extrinsicness clause is the familiar extrinsic or Cambridge-property move from the divine-simplicity literature (Grant, Brower, Stump–Kretzmann), and the eternalist, libertarian framing does no independent work. Whether 'God knows that Elias drinks' can vary across worlds while the essence stays fixed depends only on whether divine knowing is extrinsic; that holds or fails regardless of eternalism or the Anselmian openness of the act. Two of the paper's moves also fail. Under simplicity, God's will is God's essence, so dependence on 'God's contingent creative will' is not a safe intra-divine contrast case; it is the same problem. And 'if X then X' necessities concern whether the act is necessitated given the knowledge, not whether the essence varies across worlds, so they cannot show that no contingency enters the essence. The paper's claim to novelty therefore collapses into a restatement of the generic extrinsic model, with an asymmetry that does not hold.
assessment.what_it_needs: The paper must show a concrete case where an eternalist, libertarian Grounding Principle needs a different extrinsicness condition than the standard extrinsic model already gives for God's free creative choice, and why the asymmetry survives the identity of will and essence under simplicity. It should drop the misused 'if X then X' argument, engage Rogers's own defence of simplicity alongside Grant, Brower and Mullins, and answer the charge that purely extrinsic divine knowledge leaves God's knowing as a Cambridge property rather than knowledge.
assessment.summary: A competent reader would see this as the standard extrinsic-model answer to simplicity, relabelled as eternalist and libertarian without showing that those features matter, so it needs a real distinctive argument before it is a paper.
